```{r}
#| label: panel-facts
#| include: false
# The country-year panel, 270 country-years rebuilt from the GESIS waves; n_cy counts

panel_short <- readr::read_csv("../data/europeanisation_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## The question and the items {#the-question-and-the-items .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The **Standard Eurobarometer**: face-to-face interviews in every member state, about a thousand per country in each wave, a new sample every time, archived by GESIS
- One question, **"What does the European Union mean to you personally?"**, with a card of fourteen meanings; every item that the respondent picks is recorded
- The original author (OA) set the 'Euro' aside and sorted the other thirteen into four framing scales, which cross the valence of a meaning with its content:
:::

::: {.fs-70}
| Dimension | Items, with the pooled share of respondents who mentioned each |
|:--|:--|
| Cosmopolitan (positive, non-materialist) | Peace (28.54%), Democracy (21.86%), Freedom to travel, study and work anywhere in the EU (50.99%), Cultural diversity (22.12%), Stronger say in the world (23.14%) |
| Utilitarian (positive, materialist) | Economic prosperity (18.66%), Social protection (11.93%) |
| Communitarian (negative, non-materialist) | Loss of our cultural identity (12.06%), More crime (17.50%), Not enough control at external borders (16.61%), Unemployment (16.64%) |
| Libertarian (negative, materialist) | Bureaucracy (21.51%), Waste of money (21.64%) |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A scale is a **share of mentions**: "the sum of the mentioned items belonging to the specific framing dimension, divided by the total number of items mentioned by the respondent" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]
:::

::: notes
The data are the Standard Eurobarometer, the survey of the European Commission, with face-to-face interviews, about a thousand in each country and wave, and a new sample every time, so that we follow change in populations and never in persons. The outcome comes from one question, "What does the European Union mean to you personally?", asked with a card of fourteen meanings, and every meaning that the respondent picks is recorded. The original author set the euro aside and sorted the other thirteen into four scales, which cross the valence of a meaning with its content, and the robustness study named the cosmopolitan scale as the outcome. [advance] A scale is a share: the items of one dimension that a respondent mentions, divided by all the items that the same respondent mentions. Several decisions of the second half concern that definition.
:::

## The scales and the panel {#the-scales-and-the-panel .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **16 waves, 2004–2013**, the crisis decade, in the **27** member states of the time; OA modelled about **390,000** respondents in three levels, respondents in country-waves in countries
- The workshop works on the **country-year panel**: the four scales averaged within each country and year, **`r nrow(panel_short)` country-years** built from **`r format(sum(panel_short$n_cy), big.mark = ",")`** respondents, with the national **unemployment rate** and **GDP growth** beside them
:::

::: {.fs-70}
| Column | What it is |
|:--|:--|
| `cntry`, `year` | the cell |
| `mcosmo`, `mutil`, `mcomm`, `mlib` | the four framing scales, averaged in the cell, 0–1 |
| `mpos`, `mneg` | the two composites: all positive items, all negative items |
| `unemp`, `growth` | national unemployment rate and GDP growth, World Bank series |
| `n_cy` | the respondents behind the cell, from `r format(min(panel_short$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` to `r format(max(panel_short$n_cy), big.mark = ",")` |
| `bailout` | 1 if an EU/IMF assistance programme was running |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The panel addresses the **contextual** question, whether the framing of a country moves with its unemployment; the **compositional** one, whether the same people changed or the mix of people did, needs the respondents.
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic [pp. 622–625]; `data/europeanisation_cy.csv`, with its codebook.
:::

::: notes
The sixteen waves between 2004 and 2013, in the twenty-seven member states of the time, gave the original author about three hundred and ninety thousand respondents, modelled in three levels. GESIS does not allow its Eurobarometer files to be passed on, so the workshop works on an aggregate that I built from them and may share: the four scales averaged within each country and year, two hundred and seventy country-years from more than four hundred thousand interviews, those who mentioned nothing included, with the national unemployment rate and GDP growth beside them. These slides have loaded that file for you. The column `n_cy` counts the respondents behind each cell, and whether a cell should count by its respondents is one of the decisions of the second half. [advance] A panel of country means answers the contextual question only, and it cannot tell whether the same people changed or the mix of people did.
:::

## The model and the claim {#the-model-and-the-claim .smaller}

::: {.claimcard}
"… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing"

<span class="src">Teney (2016: 619), the claim as the robustness study gave it to the analysts</span>
:::

::: {.small}
- The hypothesis of the paper reads differently: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621]
- **Model 1** of Table 3: unemployment on the cosmopolitan scale, **b = −0.00340, t = −4.03, p < .001**, in a three-level model with sex, age, education, occupation, type of community, GDP growth, and the interactions of each economic indicator with education
- **Model 2** adds the variables on EU policies and party positions, and the same coefficient falls to **−0.00138, t = −1.54**
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Within one paper, support for the claim depends on which of the two models you read, and the paper reports both.
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic [pp. 619, 621, 626–627].
:::

::: notes
This is the claim as every analyst of the robustness study received it, cut from the abstract. The hypothesis of the paper reads differently and has two parts, and the second, on the materialist dimensions, never reached us, so the choice of the sentence to be tested was made before any analyst opened the data. The number behind the claim is one coefficient from Model 1 of Table 3, unemployment on the cosmopolitan scale at minus point zero zero three four, with a t of minus four, in a three-level model with individual controls, GDP growth and interactions of each economic indicator with education, which make that coefficient the slope for the lowest band of education. Model 2 adds the variables on EU policies and party positions, and the same coefficient falls to less than half and loses its significance. [advance] I read this as a choice that the paper leaves open, since it reports both models.
:::

## The record in SCORE {#the-record-in-score .smaller}

::: {.small}
SCORE put the paper through every kind of repetition on the grid:

- **Reproduction**, in the SCORE reproducibility study, with the Stata code that OA supplied on request: the push-button attempt failed before it produced a number, because the file names in the code did not match the files available for download, and the attempt that rebuilt the data from source was recorded as **'not reproduced'**
- **Robustness**: the five reanalyses of the robustness study that you have just met, unanimous on direction and more than sevenfold apart in size
- **Replication**, in the SCORE replicability study, on fourteen later Standard Eurobarometer waves fielded between 2013 and 2019: verdict **'not successful'** by the criterion that SCORE set in advance, a negative coefficient significant at 5%
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Three verdicts on one paper, one for each cell of the grid. The one that five careful people disagreed about is the one that we can work on today.
:::

::: {.src}
The SCORE dossier on the paper, [osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432); @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
SCORE put this paper through every cell of the grid, and the whole dossier is public at the address on the slide. For the SCORE reproducibility study, the original author supplied the two Stata do-files on request but could not share the data, which the GESIS terms do not allow. The push-button attempt failed before it produced a number, because the file names in the code did not match the files available for download, and the attempt that rebuilt the data from source could not recover the published effect size, so it was recorded as 'not reproduced'. The five reanalyses of the robustness study agreed on the sign and were more than sevenfold apart in size. The replication in the SCORE replicability study, on fourteen later Standard Eurobarometer waves, was judged 'not successful' by the criterion that SCORE had set in advance. [advance] The robustness verdict is the one on which five careful analysts came apart, and it is the one that we can work on today.
:::
